analysis.one_liner: Requires Pentagon PFAS contamination cleanups to meet the strictest applicable safety standard.
analysis.headline: Introduced with a single cosponsor, the bill was sent to three House committees, never received a markup or a vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: PFAS are long-lasting 'forever chemicals' used in firefighting foam and other products, and military bases are a major source of contamination of nearby drinking water. This bill would require the Department of Defense to clean up PFAS from Defense Department and National Guard activities to the most stringent of three standards: the state's standard, the federal standard, or a Safe Drinking Water Act health advisory. It died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near Defense Department and National Guard installations, especially households whose drinking water or private wells are contaminated with PFAS from military firefighting foam. Their cleanup would have to meet the strictest applicable health standard rather than a weaker one.

how_it_helps.text: Requires Defense Department response actions for PFAS contamination to achieve a level that meets or exceeds the most stringent of three benchmarks: the state standard under CERCLA, the federal CERCLA standard, or a Safe Drinking Water Act health advisory.
Applies to contamination from both Department of Defense and National Guard activities, in any environmental media.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through the Pentagon's environmental cleanup budget, since stricter cleanup levels generally cost more. The bill does not change PFAS manufacturers' existing liability under the Superfund law.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers via Pentagon cleanup budgets

drawbacks.text: The savings clause limits the bill's effect: except for the specific cleanup level required, it does not change the application of CERCLA, so it does not expand legal liability for polluters beyond existing law.

Meeting the most stringent of the three standards — including Safe Drinking Water Act health advisories, which can be set at very low, precautionary levels — would raise the cost of cleanup, borne by taxpayers through the Defense Department budget.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For communities whose drinking water is contaminated with PFAS, the benefit — cleaner water meeting the toughest applicable health standard — is direct and large. The cost is higher federal cleanup spending, which is real but spread across all taxpayers. The bill is narrow by design: it sets a cleanup level and leaves the rest of existing law untouched.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees and then to a subcommittee, and no committee ever voted on it or sent it to the floor before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Elissa Slotkin introduced the bill on August 6, 2021, with Rep. Ro Khanna as its one cosponsor.
It was referred to the Armed Services Committee and, in addition, to the Transportation and Infrastructure and Energy and Commerce Committees.
Three days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote, and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Department of Defense is better off, since it faces no new requirement to clean up PFAS to the strictest applicable health standard, and the Pentagon's cleanup budget was not increased. Communities near military installations did not get the stronger cleanup guarantee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Pentagon and its cleanup budget

for.name: Rep. Ro Khanna
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; he was its only cosponsor.

against.name: House Armed Services Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill; it never received a markup or a vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Democrats and no vote was ever taken, so no party split on the merits is recorded.

industries.note: The bill would force the Pentagon to clean up PFAS contamination to the strictest of three standards, raising its remediation costs. Those cheaper-cleanup interests run against nearby residents who want their water cleaned to a health-based level.
Stricter mandatory cleanup levels would mean more extensive, higher-standard remediation work, which federal cleanup contractors would be hired to perform.
The bill does not change manufacturers' liability: its savings clause says that except for the required cleanup level, nothing in it affects the application of CERCLA, the Superfund liability law.
